utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Witness P, my name is Bob Stein, and I represent Dario Kordic. If there is any question that I ask you that you don't understand, will you let me know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's start out by talking about the context in which the events you described in your direct examination took place. In November of 1990, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in place; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But by April 1992, the centre of that government, Sarajevo, was under siege; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: During -- it started in April of 1992, the siege of Sarajevo; April 6, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so, but I know that I went to Sarajevo on the 26th of April, 1992; I entered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Nonetheless, sir, would you agree that the Serbian army had surrounded Sarajevo in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And can we further agree that the government which was centred in Sarajevo had basically ground to a halt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot agree on that point, because the government did not stop functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not clear. The ministers and officers of the government were trapped inside of Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way, that they were in a kind of trap.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And certainly the government was not operating in the same manner in April of '92 as it was in March of '92?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. It was operating under more difficult conditions than those that prevailed in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. And furthermore, because of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, refugees started to flood various areas of the country; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, as a result of all of these things that were happening, you, on the local level, were struggling with how to manage under these adverse conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And part of that struggle was a political struggle as to what was to happen on the local level in terms of local affairs and local government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Another way of saying the same thing, perhaps, is to say there was almost a power vacuum; do you understand that term?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether one could say there was a power vacuum, or was it rather an attempt to suspend the government, which had been functioning until then, on the part of one party. In this case these were efforts made by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, if I understand your question -- let me rephrase my question. Your party, the HDZ, were all struggling to figure out how to function in the summer of 1992 in the absence of an active central government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our party was endeavouring to preserve government such as it was until then. Of course, connections with the central government were poor at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And one of the issues during the summer of 1992 is whether there would be a BiH at all, and what it would look like after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was present at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And if I understand your positions correctly,

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: (redacted) during that particular time frame, the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And do I also take it, sir, that regardless of your position, you had no military power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any military power.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At one point in time, Mr. Refik Lendo became appointed as head of the military in your area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Refik Lendo was appointed on the 25th of May, 1992, as commander of the Territorial Defence staff in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he had been a former JNA major; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He had also been in the Yugoslav intelligence service, the KOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of those things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But we can agree, can we not, that the times called out for a strong Muslim military leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those times required strong men in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. One other issue that I want to resolve: By April 1992, we can agree, can we not, that one-third of your country, one-third of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the Serb one-third, and their party -- boycotted the referendum on independence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. A very small number of Serbs took part in the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The Serb attitude during the summer of 1992 -- that is, the Bosnian Serb attitude -- is that they wanted to remain part of Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a great deal of testimony relative to Bratstvo from you and other witnesses. I want to turn your attention to some of those issues. The Croat complaint relative to the arms from Bratstvo was that those arms were being given to the JNA, who were then fighting in Croatia against the Republic of Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the summer of 1992, the JNA were using arms from Bratstvo not only against the Croats in Croatia but against the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As a result of this kind of use or misuse, depending on your perspective, of arms from Bratstvo, can we agree that in April of 1992 there were 24 truckloads of arms that were sent from Bratstvo to the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, of the 24 truckloads that were sent to the Territorial Defence or where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I have the number wrong, but in April of 1992, there were arms escorted through the Lasva Valley by the chief of police of Novi Travnik, and he was escorted, or the head of the convoy, by a Muslim. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that something like that happened, but I know that the weapons were taken both for the needs of the Croats and for the needs of the Muslims, the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Who were both fighting the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, the arms went to Visoko; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the arms went. I saw documents which said that some went to Kiseljak, to Croats and Bosniaks; to Vitez; Busovaca; Travnik. I was a witness of this. I saw this. I'm not aware that the weapons went to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You saw the video or you saw the shipment, the convoy itself? Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the papers, the documents, and I saw the people doing the driving. I saw a document, for instance, signed by Minister Jerko Doko, and the weapons were to have been taken over by Mr. Ivica Santic for the needs of the Territorial Defence of Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresevo. Therefore, all those weapons went for the Croats because he took them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the head of the convoy was a Muslim, was he not, named Cengic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding this convoy led by Cengic, I don't know, but if Cengic did come, I know that Zlatan Civcija, as chief of police, would escort the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, it's fair enough, certainly by the summer or by March 1992, the former Yugoslavia no longer existed; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that the federal laws were no longer binding on you and the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, there's been testimony in the Tribunal about these rocket launchers. Those ultimately ended up in Croat hands after some negotiations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not witness those negotiations, and I don't know where those rocket launchers ended up. I am not familiar with the negotiations over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused. You testified yesterday about those rocket launchers. Was your testimony based on what you saw or what someone else told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know that those rocket launchers were taken away, but I don't know where they went. I know they went towards Herzegovina, towards Croatia. Those are the VBRs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was less than clear. Were you aware of the negotiations that led up to those rocket launchers being taken from the Bratstvo factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of those negotiations. I know that Kordic came to my office in the evening with certain people and with his escort, and he finished the job in Bratstvo. He drove away the weapons. Where he took them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were taken towards Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Not my question. I'm not concerned where they were taken. Short and simple is: You don't know how it was that Dario Kordic came into possession of those rocket launchers, whether it was by negotiation, liberation, or any other way; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to my office. From my office he went to Bratstvo and took off those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The Court's attention is drawn to the testimony of Witness C, and there's another witness right after him that amplified this issue. I'm not going to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you perhaps aware, sir, that at the end of 1992 there was negotiations, at a very high level, between the Muslims and the Croats, regarding not only the payment for the rocket launchers but the payment for the arms that were in the convoy we talked about earlier? Were you aware of those negotiations, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about those negotiations, nor do I know where they were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So as to whether or not there was an accounting balancing the rocket launchers and the convoy's arms, you're unaware; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been such negotiations, but I was not a part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Have you heard about those, sir, from any other source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later on that there were some negotiations. Where and when and in what period, I don't know, but I heard about this sometime in 1994, that in the Defence Ministry there were discussions as to how payment should be made to the factory for everything that had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So I take your answer correctly, in 1994 you learned that at the Defence Ministry there had been some negotiations and some reconciliations relative to the payment for the rocket launchers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the final outcome was, but I was told that there were some talks. How they ended, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. You mentioned when Mr. Kordic came to Bratstvo, he was dressed in a uniform. What you meant was some sort of camouflage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a camouflage uniform he came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Later on you saw him at his headquarters. He was also wearing camouflage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Tisovac, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You never saw Mr. Kordic in a military uniform -- and by "military uniform," I mean something blue or red -- a formal military uniform; you only saw him in camouflage. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a camouflage uniform. I saw him very frequently wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So when you use the term "camouflage," you use the term "uniform" interchangeably; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a military uniform. It was a camouflage uniform with HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Lots of people, by the way, wore camouflage during 1992 and 1993, who were not associated with the military; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly this indicated military membership.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question was: Even though people were not in the military, many chose to wear camouflage: Correct, or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you. Camouflage uniforms were mostly worn by soldiers. There were exceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Stein. I should like to ask the witness whether, on this camouflage, there were insignia or indication of any military rank which Dario Kordic may have worn, indicating the rank he had in the army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember seeing the man with an indication of any rank. I remember Kostroman, his friend, who wore patches with the indication "Zenga," the national guards. That, I did see in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I don't want to burden this particular issue much. There has been testimony that even women in heels wore camouflage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stein, the witness has disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever wear camouflage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I, too, wore a camouflage uniform, but I was not a member of any military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned seeing some documents at the Grand Cafe, and there was discussion at that point in time -- this is June of '92 -- about who would be in charge, the HVO or your party; do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I remember the day when I was in the Grand Cafe; and when I was shown that document, I was concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has said that he wore a camouflage uniform although he was not a member of the military. I want to find out why he would wear a camouflage uniform even though he wasn't a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I would put it on for purely practical reasons, because I had to go on foot to headquarters in Novi Travnik, and this was a two- to two-and-a-half-hour walk from my house, and I had to go through the woods, through mud, so I wore it for practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are those practical reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was only rarely, because if you wore a normal suit, branches would tear it as you passed through the woods. And for easier maintenance. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Where did you get the uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the uniform from a friend of mine, or from my brother, who was then a member of the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So you got it from the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used mostly my brother's uniform, as I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I want to get back to this document that you were shown. How long a chance did you have to look at it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have looked at it for as long as I wanted. It was shown to me; it was on the table in front of me in the cafe. I could read it clearly and see what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How long did you choose to look at it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it through, understood the message of the document, and I examined it. I don't remember for how long. We sat there and had coffee; maybe for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But you don't recall who signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I know it was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and my opinion was that it was signed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in those days, Mr. Boban. It may have also been by Dario Kordic, but I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So now you're just guessing as to who it was signed by; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly who signed it. I know it was one of the two; that is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, you told the Court that in those days, the political and military leadership of the HDZ was together. Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion, that it was one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That opinion is not based on any study of the organisational documents of the HDZ; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my opinion, on the basis of my own experiences under those authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about, sir. You never saw any documents showing the structure of the HDZ; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at the constitution or the statute, whatever it was called, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I did read that, and I saw how the authorities were organised, and I saw that that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When did you read that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I read it sometime at the end of '92 or the beginning of '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And when was that document created, regardless of when you read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of May 1992. I really do not remember, but I know that I had the document in my hands and that I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And as to whether or not that structure changed or was modified, those were issues that you were not privy to; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the people changed in the municipal HVO in Novi Travnik. I saw those changes. I know that the first president was Zvonko Grabovac. After that it was Jozo Sekic who took over as president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But my question is not with the people. The organisation, the documents, the internal workings of that organisation were unknown to you, then and now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in May of '92 you were sent by civil authorities to talk to Dario Kordic. Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I personally knew Hasan Efendic, the TO staff commander, and Munir Jahic, who was the Minister of Urban Affairs at the time. They managed to get through to me and asked me to go to Busovaca and see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They wanted you to go to Busovaca to find out what happened in Busovaca? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted me to go to Dario Kordic to talk to him about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And then to report back to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, before you got there, you indicated you were stopped. My question is, were there other checkpoints -- let me rephrase the question. There were other checkpoints between Novi Travnik and Busovaca, were there not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall where they all were, and I don't even recall whether there were checkpoints. I only remember that one checkpoint, where I could not pass without control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, as to you going to see Mr. Kordic, you don't know what Mr. Kordic said to the soldier who was stopping you, or whether it was Mr. Kordic at all who was speaking with him; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, and I heard clearly, that the soldier to whom I introduced myself and to whom I had given my personal ID had announced me, and on the other end, I heard the response clearly, the words of another person, another soldier: "Send over the Turk," cursing my mother, "so that we can cut his throat." And they said that if Dario Kordic had guaranteed for me, that I could pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So whether these soldiers bowed to Mr. Kordic's civil influence or other authority, you can't say, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clearly a part of the military organisation. They wore military uniforms and they had military communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't clear. As to whether or not Kordic himself got on the phone, or the radio, you have no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to him. I only received permission to come to see him in Tisovac. The soldiers were the ones who were talking. What I heard was spoken by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And whether those soldiers were allowing you to pass because of an order from Mr. Kordic or a request, you don't know which; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. After they received the permission for me to pass through, I did pass through and went over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll move on. Mr. Kordic met with you for about an hour; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he told you what had happened in Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he told you about the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in Busovaca, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He said that the problem -- or at least one of the problems -- between the Muslims and the Croats was the issue of arms from Kaonik; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall those issues, the arms from Kaonik. I know that Muslims are not willing to place themselves under the HVO authority, and that this is what had to happen. He also mentioned some extremists who did not mean well to the Croatian population in Busovaca. This is how he called them, and also this is how Ignac Kostroman, who was there with him, referred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They also told you that the Muslims had reneged on an arms deal for a 50-50 split from the Kaonik JNA location; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that. I do not recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Kordic was very candid, very open with you, about all the events in Busovaca that led to what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that our conversation was very open and very candid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And at the end of that conversation, Mr. Kordic essentially said, "We're going to look out for ourselves and our Croat brothers in Bosnia-Herzegovina"; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he also said that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had to be established regardless of whether we liked it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's just take the first part. You agree with me that he said his interest was his people; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Similarly, you can agree, at that time, your interest was your people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. But it was the interest of the other people; in other words, we did not only -- we were not only concerned about our own population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You, however, as a representative of your political party, had to be concerned with the Muslim interests in Novi Travnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already stated that in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What was going to happen in this power vacuum essentially was the Croats would take care of their people; you'd take care of the interest of your people; you would meet, negotiate, and hopefully resolve things, all against the background of the Serbs surrounding you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is approximately how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, on May 28th, you mentioned you saw another document. Do you recall your testimony relative to that, the May 28th document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it. This is a document signed by Mr. Kordic, and it regards the appointment of the HVO authority in Travnik, headed by Mr. Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you keep a copy of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I copied this document which I saw at the centre for information. I made a copy for myself. I know most of the people in that HVO government. I cannot name all of them now and all the positions, but I knew exactly who was in which position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When you say "made a copy," is that a photocopy or a handwritten copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. A handwritten copy. I made notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What happened to those notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document in my possession at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But not with you here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. These were my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators from the Tribunal, and I'm referencing page 3, paragraph -- the first full -- paragraph 2, the second full paragraph on page 3, you make no mention of this document. Any reason why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention this document to the investigators, but I had given -- I had mentioned it and I gave all the names. I gave the full list of all the names of the HVO government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. In any event, at that point in time, that's 1992 May, there was also a similar government for the Muslims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The government for Muslims at that time did not exist. We insisted and asked that the presidency of the municipality be functioning; in other words, that the government be in operation, such as were elected during the democratic elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, under those elections, the HDZ was the majority party; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And under that theory, if I understand it, they would pick the government; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not do so, because we had a democratic government, and out of 60 deputies, at that time the HDZ had 20. In other words, HDZ could not form its own government without other parties. There were SDA, SPS, SDS, SDP. There were representatives of Serbs, six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's been appropriately commented this is not a case about politics, so I don't want to go deeply into this. Let me go back to my first question. When did you start your own government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosniaks established their own government in late August or early September in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a representative of that government. I had no -- I held no position in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So by the end of the summer or early fall of 1992, in Novi Travnik, there were two governments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to move forward to June 19. Who was the head of the -- who was the Muslim head of propaganda and information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we had a head for propaganda and information in that period around 19 June 1992. I don't know whether the TO headquarters had that position or not. I really could not say. There was no such position in the civilian bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As to the military bodies, you wouldn't know whether there was that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know this, not for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's get back to this June 1992 meeting. There were three political representatives for your side; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: June 1992, I remember that it was myself, I think Muharem Haskic, and I don't know who else was with me. That was the morning, and I also know who was there in the afternoon. On 19 June, two meetings were held: one in Jozo Sekic's office, the president of the municipality; and the other one with Zvonimir Grabovac, the HVO head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the afternoon meeting. In the afternoon meeting, from your side were three civilian representatives and two military representatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And on the Croat side, the HDZ, there were three political representatives and two military representatives; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Separated out political and military, right, just like you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I want to be very clear on this. According to your statement: "The HDZ also had three political reps," and you name them, "and two military reps," and then you name them. Three and two; civil, military. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I believe that this was so. I believe that that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, this is a question that I pondered many times: In the middle of this civil war in June 1992, whose laws were you following, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not agree on the fact that in June 1992 there was a civil war. The laws that we followed were the laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the laws which were adopted from the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That was the Muslim position. The Croats took a different position, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was obviously the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, during these negotiations, as I understand it, in this area where the last formal legitimate legal election resulted in the HDZ having the majority party, the HDZ took the position that based on that, you and your party should be under them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were precisely their positions, that they are the main party, they were the majority population, and that we needed to subordinate ourselves to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And in other areas, based on your knowledge of what was going on, where they were the minority party, they were willing to submit themselves to the TO and be under them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not so. That was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. You mentioned in your direct-examination that you actually called General Merdan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You had access to his phone or Motorola and just picked them up and called him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sitting together with the Croatian negotiating team, and I had access to a telephone there. After I heard through the centre for information that the regional TO staff from Zenica had given instructions to the TO to subordinate themselves to the HVO, then I asked to be -- that I be given contact, and after I reached Dzemal Merdan he said that this is not so, and we wanted to ask for an unconditional cessation of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, regardless of the fact that you had phone access to General Merdan, that access didn't make you part of the military suddenly, did it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's a matter that the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May I rephrase, Judge? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Just because you had military contacts, you didn't have a military position at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no military position at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And because of that position you wanted to know what the military was doing, and they you, but that didn't mean that you had command authority over the military; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no command authority over the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's also true that you wanted to know what was going on on the military side, and they wanted to know what was going on on the civil side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about the soldiers that you talked with in June of 1992, and I want to make sure that we're talking about the same thing. Do you claim that you yourself spoke to ten HVO soldiers in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to all ten of them, but I talked to the majority among the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What kind of shape were they in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that they were in very good shape, but they were a bit scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the statement that you gave to the Tribunal investigators, but before I ask that, did these men give written statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question and make it easier. On page 5 of your statement to the investigators from the Tribunal, you say, and I quote, and this is from the third full paragraph: "During the first attack in June of 1992, approximately ten HVO soldiers from Busovaca were arrested. They provided statements in which they claim that Kordic sent soldiers from Busovaca to Novi Travnik. I believe our local 708th Brigade or department of security would have these statements. The police chief, Sejbid Corbic [phoen], might have the statements." Now, I ask you again, sir, isn't it a fact that the statements were in writing and given to someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my conversation with them, this was the answer that I received, and I assumed that the people in the Territorial Defence had taken their written statements at that time. So this is my opinion, and this is why I stated it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you never told the investigators from the Tribunal that you, yourself, spoke with the soldiers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that I had spoken to them, and I still say that I personally had spoken to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the investigator from the Tribunal didn't put it down in your statement; is that probably what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just read out that I had talked to them. It is written in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk about Marinko Marelja -- but I'm reminded, before I do: Can you give us the names of the soldiers with whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers from Busovaca? I don't know any of those names. I know they were all sort of shortish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you able to determine their rank or their unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not determine it. I only saw that they were wearing camouflage uniforms and that they were scared, because they had been there for about ten hours by then. They had spent the whole night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, getting back to my question: Marinko Marelja, his various positions have been described in your direct testimony. We can agree, can we not, that he, like you, was involved with the civil authorities of government; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that. I did this as a professional, and he at that time was doing it as a volunteer, on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he, like you, had no control over the military; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, he was not in the military. I am not aware of him being a member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, we can also agree that in June, July, and August of 1992, Muslim refugees started coming into Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree that in this period -- that is, May, June, July -- May, June, July, and then August through October -- refugees had stayed in Novi Travnik, not only the Muslims who had fled, but also Croats. They were in the Sports Hall and also in the kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And we can also agree that the Muslim refugees were registered by the government of Novi Travnik as citizens of Novi Travnik, given identification cards, et cetera; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't agree on that. We could agree that they were registered, because there was a coordinating committee who was taking care of that, and this was -- it was appointed by the joint government headed by Jozo Sekic. So this was a joint body which cared for the refugees who were streaming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And by "registered," do you mean registered as citizens of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were registered as displaced persons in that period. Nobody gave them any ID cards; therefore, there could be no talk about the change of the population structure in favour of the Muslims in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, you hit on something I was going to ask you: If, indeed, they had been registered as citizens of Novi Travnik, that would have changed the political lay of the land; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. That was not the case. A joint body was in charge about those people, and they registered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I heard your answer, and I understand it. My question, though, is: If in fact they had been registered, that would have changed the political lay of the land; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us know how many Muslims and how many Croats, or rather how many Bosniak displaced persons and how many Croat displaced persons, arrived. I do not have those figures, but I assume that these figures can be checked in the municipality even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, sir, we need not debate or hang on here much longer. My question really boils down to: The refugees were given homes that the Serbs had vacated in your town, Novi Travnik, during this period of time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not right at all. The refugees from Novi Travnik mainly went to Croatia and to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the refugees, the Muslim refugees who began coming into Novi Travnik during this period of time, started their own police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot agree about that because it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, however, by the end of the summer of 1992, Novi Travnik was divided; there was a Croat side and there was a Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that already with regard to the authorities. The government was formed sometime in August 1992. We cannot say that Novi Travnik was totally divided in that time frame. It became completely divided sometime in June or July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My question wasn't precise. In June or July of 1993, the geography, the physical lay of the land in Novi Travnik, was such that there was a Croat side and a Muslim side; is that right? Is that what I just heard you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By then, that was how it was. There was a Croatian and a Bosniak side within the framework of the territory of Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And do I take it that the two gas stations in Novi Travnik, the two petrol stations, were in the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two petrol stations were left on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And of course one of the issues in June of 1992 was access to petrol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in June '92. There was no question of access to petrol. At least, I'm not aware of it, and I was active and present there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did that become an issue later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told when I returned from Zagreb that there were problems during the conflict in October '92, allegedly something to do with the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I take it these things were told to you by others, and you weren't present during that point of time, in which case I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I only heard this from others. I wasn't there, so I can't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about the rally in which Mr. Kordic was present. First of all, you were invited to that rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited to that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There was nothing secret about that rally; everyone could come and see. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everyone could come and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And what Mr. Kordic said was that the HVO was being restructured; isn't that right? Changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he spoke about the organisation of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And as I understand it, the TO also, from time to time, would administer oaths, loyalty oaths, to its members; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, two or three days prior to that, had its own meeting in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Same place, same kind of meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same place, same place. In front of the municipality building in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Same kind of oath-taking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly of a different content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course the words were different, but the effect was the same; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could agree about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were told that the military people surrounding Dario Kordic were members of the Jokers unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I was told by Croats who were there, when I asked. The people carrying flags reminded me of the people who were in Novi Travnik that we have spoken about who had been arrested. They were all shortish, and I was told that they were Kordic's Jokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On behalf of the short people in the world, I'm -- my question to you, sir: The person who told you, do you know the name of the individual who told you that this unit was in fact called the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several people who were with me. For example, like President Sekic, Ovlatovic [phoen], who later on went with us to the hotel. This is funny, but indeed, those people were short in stature, so they reminded me of the people who had been arrested previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that in fact the Jokers unit had not been established till January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I don't know that. I know what I was told: that those were Kordic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you told they were Kordic's men, or were you specifically told the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kordic's. Kordic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. So you were told these were Kordic's men, not that the name of the unit was the Jokers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether they gave me the name of the unit. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On or about October 13th, 1992, Alija Izetbegovic visited Novi Travnik, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he came in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he visited only Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at that meeting, and I don't know where and whom he visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In your travels and in your positions, did you hear that Mr. Izetbegovic's visit in October of 1992 included any visits to any Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later heard that he was in the Territorial Defence headquarters and that he spoke there with representatives. I wasn't present, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, therefore, although the president was in Travnik [sic], he spoke to the TO and to Muslims, and you know of no instances in which he spoke to the HDZ or the Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether he had any such talks. As I said, I wasn't there. I wasn't in town, in fact, I think, so I don't know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And for the record, I've been appropriately corrected: I've been using "Travnik," and I've been meaning "Novi Travnik," and that's what we've been talking about. By the way, are you related by blood or by marriage to President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not related to that family in any way, by blood or marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, as to seeing a tape of Mr. Kordic in Novi Travnik when you came back from Zagreb, first, what were you doing in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Minister Munir Jahic, who invited me to take over some documents from him. He was in a hotel in Zagreb. According to what I saw, he left upon orders of the Prime Minister, Jure Pelivan. The documents I took over had to do with the accommodation of refugees in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Minister Jahic is the Bosnian Minister for what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: For urban planning and the environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jahic Munir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The tape you saw was a tape that someone did with a hand camera or that was taken from television or what, the video cassette that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly where it was filmed, but I think it must have been done by an amateur, but I saw it personally, asking Refik Lendo for a delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As to whether that tape was made on October 23rd, 22nd, 21st, or 20th, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the tape was made, because I arrived in Novi Travnik from Zagreb on the 24th of October. It was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on. Do you consider yourself to have friendly connections with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I was on friendly terms with Dario Kordic, but I think we knew one another quite well. I think we met sometime in 1991, but I can't exactly remember where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask is you've had coffee with Mr. Kordic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I had coffee with Mr. Kordic and with Marelja. A cafe I often went to was on the way from my apartment to the municipality building where I worked. But in view of the fact that Kordic was on exceptional good terms with Marinko Marelja, we would meet often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But my point is: Simply because you were seen having coffee with Marelja and/or Kordic didn't mean that you were all fast, good friends, did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you could make such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Therefore, we can agree, can we not, that even if Mr. Kordic and Mr. Marelja had coffee and were seen together, that doesn't necessarily make them fast, good friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to the end of your testimony, in which you said that certain gentlemen said frequently that they would always have to ask of their superiors or their commanders when you were negotiating. Do you remember that part, when the Judge was asking you some questions? Remember that part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were negotiating with the gentlemen, as you say, who were on the civil side of what was happening in Bosnia; isn't that right? You weren't negotiating with the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mostly sought negotiators in members of the HDZ of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: These individuals told you they had to report to their higher level authority on the civil side; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a frequent answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And those three men that you mentioned were all civilians. Mr. Sekic -- and the transcript doesn't say the other names -- Zoran Matosevic, they're all civilian --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Matosevic, not Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Either I mispronounced it or it was written wrong. It doesn't matter. They're all civil authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: During the conflict in the summer of 1992 and into 1993, Novi Travnik had no water; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: During the summer of 1992, into 1993, Novi Travnik had no water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were occasional problems, but Novi Travnik is having problems with water even today, when there's no conflict, and the officials are well aware of that, especially the part of the town in which Bosniaks are living today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: During this same conflict, Novi Travnik had no electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. Mostly there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And no telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the access to the water, the control of the water, was from the Muslim side of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novi Travnik is supplied from two sources of water, and both of them were, conditionally speaking, under the control of the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The same thing with the electricity, under the control of the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the telephones, under control of the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the telephone was under the control of the Croats, because the post office was on the Croat side. The telephone was under Croat control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me finish this theme, and that is: During the conflict, it's fair to say that the schools in the Lasva Valley were closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were closed, yes. I don't remember exactly when they started working again in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. During the time they were closed, is it fair to say the Muslims sent their children to special Muslim schools?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that cannot be said, because I am not aware of such schools. In my municipality, there were no such schools. I don't know what schools you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm almost at the end, for Your Honours' edification. I have two more areas I'd like to go into, if I may, before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The first is -- again, I think we've covered this. You yourself, in your position and because of your position, have never given a military order to a military unit; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never given such an order, nor did I have the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certain members of the military, in response to a request from you, may do what you ask, and, in fact, have done what you've asked; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly I didn't make any such requests. I didn't do anything that I was not authorised and responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My last question is this: Can we also agree that the line that divided your town, Novi Travnik, during the conflict in 1993, still divides your town? There's still a Croat side and there's still a Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik today, there is a unified government established on the basis of the constitution of the republic and the canton. There is a municipal council in Novi Travnik presided by a Bosniak, and there is a municipal chief who is a Croat. He is the executive and he has control of the executive and the legislative. I think those divisions are gradually being overcome with the return of people to their former homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My fault for being --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the power is in these two institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My fault for being imprecise. On the ground in Novi Travnik today, in one were to walk into the streets, there would be a Croat side and a Bosniak side; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be visible for people coming from the outside and who don't know the town. Those who know where the lines were still remember them, but people are coming back and those lines are being lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, forgive me for being imprecise, but the point remains: The Bosniaks live on one side; the Croats live on the other.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly that is so, but gradually that is being overcome. I think I was quite clear. As people are returning to their homes from which they were evicted, those lines are disappearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, how long are you likely to be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think no longer than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the adjournment now. We'll sit again at half past 11.00. Mr. Kovacic, if you could stick to the half hour, we could get on with another witness. Mr. Lopez-Terres, if you could keep re-examination to an absolute minimum, it will save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May we ask who the next witness is, without revealing anything, or at least in the recess tell us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can do it in the usual way. Very well. Half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness P, my apologies for having to address you in this manner, but this is for your own protection. I am a Defence attorney for Mr. Mario Cerkez. My name is Bozidar Kovacic, and along with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, we represent this client. Towards the end of your evidence yesterday, when asked by the Prosecutor, you said that in the early months of 1993, in Novi Travnik, there were some units from Herzegovina called Bruno Busic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these men were known as Herzegovinians, and later on, we learned that they belonged to the Bruno Busic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then you also said that in Novi Travnik there was a brigade called Stjepan Tomasevic which was active there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In Novi Travnik there was also a brigade which bore the name of Stjepan Tomasevic. It was a local brigade, and its commander at the time was Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's take it one step at a time, please. Can we agree that the Bruno Busic Brigade came from outside and that the Stjepan Tomasevic was a local unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Earlier, you gave a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, on 13 September 1995, and this statement has been mentioned here today. Let me try to refresh your memory. Towards the very end of it, you said, and I quote: "I am not sure about the chain of command of the HVO military, but I know that the following people were HVO commanders in Novi Travnik." And then you mention some names: Ivica Markovic, Mario Cerkez, Borivoj Malbasic, and Zeljko Sabic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it should be Zeljko Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well; it was misspelled. And then you also added, "I am not sure of when these people acted as commanders." So from this, it would follow that in 1995, that you mentioned names of people who were in positions of command, but you did not tell specifically who was commander at what time. This is what would follow from the statement; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but today I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but would you please just answer the question: That would follow from the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I named them as I knew, but I approximately know who was commander in which period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And yesterday, during your examination, you said that Cerkez was the commander of the Tomasevic Brigade, as you said, in the early months of 1993. And from the previous sentences, it would mean that this was January or February of 1993. My question to you is: How do you recall this better and more specifically now than when you gave the statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just spoke more specifically. I recalled it then and I recall it now, that in this period, Mario Cerkez was the commander, because I met him at least on two occasions in early 1993. We attended certain meetings together. I remember the meeting which ended by the commander of the brigade I think had left with them to a restaurant, Oskar, where he was arrested and taken to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to show the witness D22/2, which is related to Witness F's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness P, will you please first focus on the line where the date is; that is, that was entered by hand. And then, please, if you can focus then on signatures, there are four signatories. Your signature is the second?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were other meetings that followed this where he was present, not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you would just please wait for the question, let us first lay the ground for it. This was one of the meetings which you had mentioned; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not one of the two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this meeting from which this report was issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we can conclude that representatives of both parties were present -- that is, both the HDZ and the SDA parties -- as well as representatives of both military organisations, the HVO and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted); and for the Novi Travnik HVO, Borivoj Malbasic signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So on 13 January, we can conclude that Borivoj Malbasic was the commander of the HVO brigade. You said that Cerkez was not present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that Cerkez was not present in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You just used the word "obvious." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not at this meeting, as can be seen from this document. I know that Cerkez succeeded Borivoj Malbasic. I don't know which period, but I know that it was before March 1993. And during this period, I attended at least two meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you don't know with respect to January and February?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about January. I don't know exactly when he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about February?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was appointed sometime in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Ismet Sahinovic told us here that Cerkez did attend the meeting on 13 January.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether he was in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But while we're at this meeting, you will agree with me that the main conflicts in Novi Travnik between the army and the HVO, one was on 19 June '92, and then 12th October 1992, and then January to July, there was a third?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From your evidence, in early 1993 and late 1992, there were tensions, and there were a number of incidents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We said that on the Croatian side, the side of the HVO, that there were units which arrived from outside of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody knows this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the Bosniak side, were there also units which came from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was a single unit other than the TO units and the BH army who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were units from Krajina there, the so-called Krajisnici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, Krajisnici were in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about Ravno and Rostovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is Ravno Rostovo? Ravno Rostovo is a village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Krajisnici were there in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know that in late 1992 and early 1993, the Krajisnici were present there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were present in Travnik, but not in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you specifically that this had to do with the 7th Muslim Brigade, which was stationed in the motel in Ravno Rostovo, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade was not present in the territory of the Novi Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's return to this area. You agree that there were tensions around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you do not agree that there were also extremists on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to, what extremists you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you agreed that there were extremists on both sides.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there extremists on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who killed and terrorised. I don't know that there were such people on our side, who persecuted people of Croat ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who kidnapped four HVO officers later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this. I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document you have in front of you. Could you please read point 1 of this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The parties, the SDA and the HDZ, take distance from all the public announcements produced by the media controlled by either of the ethnic groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why was this statement made? What did this refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had to do with the public announcements produced by the HDZ or the HVO regarding certain issues and certain positions in relation to Novi Travnik, and also had to do with certain announcements that came from the ABiH headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that they're trying to calm things down and take some distance from that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I understand it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to point 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All participants in this meeting take distance from all the excess situations and believe that strict measures should be taken against perpetrators of these incidents on both sides."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that both sides agreed that there are people who are causing these incidents on both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is obvious, because representatives of both sides are present there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can both counsel and witness slow down a little bit, because it is hard to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, there is a request from the interpreters to slow down. And Witness P, could you slow down too, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness P, my fault. The problem that we have is we understand each other well, so we engage in very fast exchanges. I'm going to try to be more mindful of it. In order not to take too much time, I think the document speaks for itself. There are further measures mentioned that both sides take upon themselves to do in order to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the usher's assistance, could I have Exhibit D2/2 shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness P, would you first please look at the heading? The document was issued on the 13th January, in Mostar, by the main headquarters. It was on the same day when this public announcement was also drafted and, according to my information, several hours after you agreed on that previous announcement. This is obviously a document which obligates the HVO units to actively engage in cooperation. Have you seen such a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Had you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. At the beginning of the conflict in Novi Travnik, in early summer or before the confrontation in June, you also mentioned that HOS was present, H-O-S, in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain who HOS was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were men wearing black uniforms. We knew them as such, and they also presented themselves as members of HOS. I know certain of them by names. Suse, and Deba, and some others, Burce [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: HOS was not a member of the HVO in Novi Travnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether HOS was ever a part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me that HOS was an independent force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with it, nor can I deny it. I don't know how they functioned. I don't know whether they were part of the HVO, but I know that they had their own uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The general view was that they were rather extremist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the general view. Also, a prevailing view was that the HVO and the HOS were very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
