utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And despite being offered the job, you turned it down; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I turned it down, because Anto Nuk, Vlatko Males, and Stipo Zigonja were with me at the -- with the TO staff, at the TO headquarters at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have previously given some testimony about your duties with the transportation unit of the TO once you had made the decision to join the TO. Actually, you later occupied a position in the military police, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was first in the military police, and then I got the post with the office for transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, in May of 1992, you were a member of the military police within the TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And one of your subordinates was Mr. Furundzija, about whom you have given evidence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a platoon commander of the military police with the municipal TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you gave evidence that you were arrested by the HVO on three separate occasions, the first being on September the 7th, 1992, or thereabouts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were arrested actually in front of the Hotel Vitez while you were in TO uniform; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Didn't you testify in Blaskic and in Aleksovski, though, that you were not wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested for the first time on the 7th, as you mentioned. At that time I was not in a uniform. But the second time, when I was captured between the cinema and the hotel on the 21st of October, then I was in the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, let me read to you what you said to the Prosecutors in January of 1997. You describe your arrest on September the 7th, 1992, and you said, on page 3: "I was uniformed when I was arrested." Were you or weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th, when there was a conflict, I was arrested in a uniform when I had to leave the TO headquarters. In fact, that was on the 21st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you were questioned by some members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was questioned along with Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Santic a member of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade or not, or do you simply not know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, because Ludvig Pavlovic unit members were wearing drab green uniforms, whereas he wore a black uniform, and I don't believe that he was a member of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. He questioned you for half an hour, and you weren't mistreated in any way, were you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Just the two of them took my cigarette case. There were two members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade took a cigarette case with some cigarettes, and Vlado Santic questioned me about some military affairs or some things which were in the TO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And ultimately, your headquarters arranged with the HVO headquarters for you to be exchanged for an HVO prisoner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the agreement was. I only know that I was exchanged. At least, I was going to -- that is what I was told, but I don't know who I was exchanged for. I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to the incident in October 1992, about which you gave some evidence. As I understand it, sir, you had been to the town of Visoko, leading an ABiH convoy in the early morning hours of October the 20th, 1992. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: After delivering your shipment, you then headed back to Vitez, to your TO headquarters, along the main road; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not a shipment; this was -- these were members of the TO which were going to provide some assistance there and go to the front lines against the JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You did -- as you've previously testified, you arrived back at your headquarters at the TO in the high school, the Boris Kidric high school, in Dubravica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Not in Dubravica; rather, in Vitez, in the secondary school centre. I don't know what was the school in Dubravica called. This was how I went back to Vitez, to the Boris Kidric centre, that secondary school centre where the command post was, where the headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's true, isn't it, that when you arrived back in your headquarters, it was surrounded by HVO troops, approximately 70 of them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know about the exact number, whether there was exactly 70, but around that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your headquarters, I believe, there were about 37 TO staff at that location; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-six or thirty-seven, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Basically, what happened was there was a stand-off for about four days and no exchange of fire between the TO and the HVO forces while negotiations occurred, that resulted in relocation of the TO headquarters from where you were to Stari Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but you said that there was no shooting on the part of the HVO, but several grenades called Zolja were lobbed into the secondary school centre and then an ultimatum followed for us to leave the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me just read from your statement four years ago, given to the Prosecution: "We stayed in our HQ for three days, during which time there was no exchange of shooting." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I said that there was no exchange of fire. We didn't shoot, we could not, but two Zolja grenades were shot at the centre. We were very few. We did not shoot, and our Major, Hakija Cengic, forbid any kind of resistance before the talks with somebody from the HVO had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the HVO permitted the TO commander, Sefkija Dzidic, and his deputy, Ramiz Dugalic, to relocate their headquarters to Stari Vitez; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He most probably did. They transferred to Stari Vitez and we -- that is, I stayed in the secondary school centre with the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were subsequently permitted, though, to load up trucks and drive them back and forth between the old headquarters location and the new headquarters in Stari Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They gave us a period of time within which we had to vacate the centre and pick up all the things that we needed and move to the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They also indicated, Lieutenant, did they not, the route that you should take to ensure safe passage?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't told anything by anyone, by the HVO. I was ordered by Sefkija Dzidic to go from the secondary school centre to the hotel, from the hotel to the marketplace, then from the market to Old Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you from the statement that you gave four years ago, sir: "On the fourth day, the HVO allowed us to load some trucks with materials from our HQ and take them to Stari Vitez. I drove the van filled with grenades through the town, instead of the road which the HVO told me to take, because I was afraid the HVO would shoot at the van." That's true as well, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but I got the route through the -- past the stadium into Old Vitez, and it was impossible to pass there. So I received an order from my superior to go through the downtown area, because the agreement was to go -- the agreement had been for us to go through the town rather than around via the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand the situation. You were driving a civilian truck that was unknown to the HVO, filled with grenades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Not a truck; a van, because -- I mean, I did not know what vehicles we had, and I did not know what vehicles the HVO had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. It was a civilian van, but it was filled with grenades, and you hadn't told the HVO about that, had you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was not in a position to say anything, because I did not take part in negotiations. I was just carrying out my commander's orders, if you understand me. I was not involved in negotiations or talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. There were also two sniper's rifles in that truck along with all of the grenades; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and a pair of military binoculars, from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also two other items, sir. There was your personal machine gun; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As well as the automatic pistol that you were wearing as a sidearm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I carried my personal pistol which was officially issued to me from JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you were apprehended and questioned again by the HVO, and on this second occasion it is also true that you were not mistreated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was not mistreated; I was just arrested and interrogated, but I was arrested by the HVO with ten RPG grenades and Zoljas, and about 15 soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The gentleman that you gave testimony about, Mr. Muhamed Patkovic, he became a Mujahedin fighter, did he not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he became later a Mujahedin fighter, but I know that that man was beaten up in the Vitez Hotel and that they even took his boots off, and that they split his ear, they beat him so badly that day when they captured him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did tell the Prosecutors four years ago that Mr. Patkovic was, in fact, with the Mujahedin, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I said that? I don't remember saying that. I really do not remember saying that. It may be an error in the translation, but I know that while he was in the TO he was not a Mujahedin, because he couldn't have been. He may have later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to belabour that point, so I'll move on. The soldiers who questioned you, sir, had told you that the HVO had actually been attacked by the TO at Ahmici, did they not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, just before April the 15th, were you aware that four HVO soldiers had been kidnapped by Mujahedin just outside of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that an assassination attempt had been made upon Darko Kraljevic on April the 12th, 1993, in the woods outside Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, to your knowledge, commanded a detachment known as the Vitezovi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And those troops only took orders from him, their commander, and nobody else; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you were asked that question, sir, in the Blaskic case, by one of the Judges, and I believe that you said, on page 2446, that Darko Kraljevic could do what he liked. On page 2425, you said these Vitezovi "only took orders from their commander and nobody else." And then one page later you said that "it was an exclusive unit, a private army. They took their orders only from their commander and nobody else," and the reference to "commander" was a reference to Darko Kraljevic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I remember all of that. However, as regards those orders, I think that every commander issues strict orders to his soldiers, and whether he personally gave such orders, I don't know; I was not in his presence. I was a member of the Territorial Defence. I was not a member of the HVO, the Vitezovi, or the Jokers, or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Did you know that the TO had a battalion headquarters at the villages of Poculica and Preocica, to the north-east of Vitez? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise; could you repeat the question, please? I didn't quite hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Certainly. It's true, is it not, that the TO had battalion headquarters at the villages of Poculica and Preocica, to the north-east of Vitez, immediately before the fighting on April the 16th?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I don't know whether the command was there. I was in the TO headquarters. I was not in the battalions. There's a difference between the staff of the Territorial Defence. I couldn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that the battalion headquarters of the 325th Mountain Brigade was located in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that when the restructuring of the TO was carried out, when it was transformed into a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when was that? That was before April the 15th, 1993, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You gave some testimony in connection with a building known as the Bungalow, and you stated that you had seen a lady that you recognised at that location. Let me just read you a statement that you gave to the Prosecution's investigators four years ago. This is on page 6: "While I was there, I did not hear or see any women at the Bungalow."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There seems to be quite a bit of misunderstanding. I have already testified. I made those statements in order, but I said in my first statement that I saw two women, one of whom I recognised, the other one I did not. The soldier on the balcony ordered those women to go back behind the balcony. I saw that and I still stick to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission -- I'm actually relatively close to being finished -- I'd just like to show the witness the statement he gave to the Prosecutors four years ago, with the usher's assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For your easy reference, sir, I've highlighted it on page 5 of the Croatian version. Thank you. Could you just read into the record, sir, the passage that I have highlighted?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: "I didn't hear or see any women in the Bungalow." That is what it says here, explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the people that you saw wearing black uniforms at the Bungalow did not have any insignia on their uniforms, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Some did, some did not. I couldn't notice everything, but I know that I saw Jokers, then I saw some police members. There were three different military units at the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you saw Mr. Vlado Santic at the Bungalow; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he was wearing a black uniform, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a black uniform, yes, with a white belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But he was not wearing any insignia, just like the rest of the people you've identified as Jokers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He did not wear any insignia on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Jokers did not wear insignia either, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The Jokers did wear the insignia of the Jokers. Anto Furundzija wore the Jokers patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you some testimony that you gave on August the 26th, 1997, sir, under oath in the Blaskic case, page 2326. " Q: How was Mr. Vlado Santic dressed when you saw him? A: He was wearing a black uniform without any insignia, like the rest of the Jokeri." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The question for Vlado was correct, because I didn't see an insignia on him. But when it says "like the other Jokers," that, I'm not sure of. But I know that Vlado did not wear an insignia, because he spoke to me for a minute or half a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've identified quite a few commanders of this unit, the first one being Mr. Vlado Santic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've identified several others, but another individual who you've previously identified as a commander was named Ivica Vujica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Vujica was a commander of the Jokers who took me to dig trenches at Kratine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you have previously testified that this man always treated you very correctly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Not Ivica Vujica, but Ivica Markovic, a civilian policeman, a refugee from Jajce. As for Ivica Vujica, he was a leader of a Jokers platoon. There is a difference between a civilian policeman and a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You really have no detailed personal knowledge of the function or purpose or complement of the Jokers unit, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have any detailed information about their purpose, but I know they were promoted in Vitez as a unit for special purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the point I'm making to you, sir, is that you really just don't know very much about the unit at all, do you, personally, from your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: It can't be said that I don't know much. I know from the moment they were founded until I met them at Kratine and in the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you were asked, "Could you please be more detailed about the Joker unit," in the Aleksovski case a few years ago, page 398, and you said, quote: "I personally don't know much about it." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying again that I personally don't know much about them, but I know how they asserted themselves in Vitez and how they introduced themselves in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Two final topics, if I may. The ribbons that you previously described, the ribbons bearing different colours: Did I understand you to say that those ribbons identified the particular task that the military unit was carrying out, and that that was actually a tradition established in the JNA, standard practice in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, that was my assumption. I didn't say that the red ribbon meant the first front line; the second, the second front line; and so on. As far as I know from the former JNA, the blue ribbon was always the defence and the red the aggressor. So the first position was marked with a red ribbon, the reserve position with a blue ribbon. I know the system from the former JNA. I didn't say now that the same applied to the HVO. These are just my assumptions. I said that this shouldn't go down in the record. Why it did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said that when you were present at the Bungalow, you saw people wearing white, orange, or blue ribbons tied around their arms; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, across their shoulders, on the epaulettes. And some wore them also on their muscles, up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you also said -- and I don't think there is any dispute about this, so let's try to agree upon it -- that the use of ribbons was copied by the HVO from the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I cannot claim that, but I know that from my military training in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And after you were released on May the 5th, I understand that you rejoined the army about two weeks later, on May the 22nd, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I underwent psychiatric examination in hospital, because I had these cramps, for ten or fifteen days. And after that I was mobilised again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of final questions. You have never met or spoken to Colonel Blaskic in your life, have you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I take it the same goes for the accused in this case, Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't even know Kordic in person. I never even saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as my colleague, Mr. Sayers, has already said, we had prepared for Witness Baggesen, as we were told yesterday. But a change occurred today, but we have somehow managed to prepare for the cross-examination, in order not to waste Your Honours' time, so with your permission, I would like to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kavazovic. My name is Mikulicic, and together with my colleague, Kovacic, I represent the Defence of Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to answer my questions to the best of your recollection, and if any of my questions is not clear, please tell me. Mr. Kavazovic, you said that you were born in the village of Vrhovine, Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you the only child?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have five brothers and a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So there were six children in all?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but one died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was your family well off?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We were a working-class family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you completed your elementary school where?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In Vitez, in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, this must be tiring for you. Please let me know if you don't feel well, and then we can do something about it. Can you continue with this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm okay, though I have a big ulcer, so it's causing me some discomfort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After an eight-year elementary school, you went to Belgrade to attend secondary military school?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had an uncle there, working in the Public Security Station, at the Danube station, district 29, married to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. So you left home, so you must have been quite a financial burden for your parents as you went away?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't for my parents, but I was for my uncle. My uncle financed me and covered the costs of education. He didn't have any children, and he was an inspector in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. Did you receive any kind of scholarship from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we received regular support to cover essential needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after completing schooling, you became a professional officer in the JNA, and you received a salary?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also had some other privileges given to JNA officers, such as free transportation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in some areas, some allowances. When we went on mission, you could spend your holidays in military holiday homes. But that was for higher-level officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, while you were in the JNA in '91 and the beginning of '92, what was your exact position?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was a traffic dispatcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where were you located?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: At Vozdovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade, district of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 18th of February, 1992, you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the help -- with a colleague of mine, a Serb, Branislav Jeknic, who was working with me and who transferred me to Kuzmin and Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. It was only the date that was interesting for me, the 18th of February. Why did you leave the JNA? I'm asking you this because the JNA gave you a job, certain privileges, and so on. Why did you abandon it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was schooled for the five-cornered star, and not for different emblems, the tricolour and a beret. Because another of my friends, a Croat, also abandoned the JNA, because the war started in Croatia, and seeing that we would be deployed as officers, we had to desert the JNA, not to be used in the war. We didn't want the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, is it true that already in '91, the JNA attacked Slovenia with tanks and aircraft?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that already in '91, Vukovar in Croatia was attacked, as well as Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All this was in full swing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA razed to the ground the village of Ravno at the end of '91?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that with precision, but I had the good fortune for my uncle to fix it for me not to be deployed anywhere else until I managed to go back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So on the 18th of February, you managed to leave?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the help of this colleague of mine who helped me get back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next set of questions. In your testimony today, and this is something you referred to in your earlier statements as well, you said that in the Vitez Hotel, on the 20th of May, 1992, Samir Trako had been killed, and that your commander, Mr. Hakija Cengic, went to the Hotel Vitez for a meeting with Mr. Cerkez, and you escorted him there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Kavazovic, that you noticed that Mr. Cerkez was wearing a black uniform with HOS patches.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time, or now, did you know what his role was, what his position was in the organisation of HOS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that he was a commander of HOS, or a section of HOS. I can't be more precise. But I do know that he held a position there, because he was able to talk with my commander. So that was a command level, so they must have been on a par.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Cengic and Mr. Cerkez, was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Anto Furundzija. Who else was inside, I don't know. I came with Cengic; I don't know who was inside. They mentioned Valenta, and I don't know whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, a moment ago in your testimony you mentioned the name of Mr. Edib Zlotrg. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We were together in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. But did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Had you heard that he was a forensic technician in the Vitez police station?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I know he worked in the administration, but I had no contact with the civilian police. I know he was in the police, a civilian policeman, and for a while I think he worked with Santic, if that is correct, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, did you know somebody called Mr. Muhamed Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because he came from my village. He was born in Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in those days, that evening, on the 20th of May, he attended a meeting in the hotel, a meeting of the crisis staff in connection with this murder? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Edib Zlotrg, as a crime technician of the Vitez police, participated in the inquest in connection with this killing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that later, but I didn't see him that evening. I just came with Cengic and Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, if I were to tell you that both these gentlemen, Mr. Zlotrg and Mujezinovic, testified in court in this Tribunal about that event, and their contact with Mr. Cerkez that evening, that both of them said that Mr. Cerkez was wearing a camouflage uniform and not a black uniform, what would be your comment? Would you still insist that he was in a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I still insist that he was in a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, you made several prior statements through the court's investigators, among them one on the 7th of May, 1993, also to the 3rd Corps of the BH army; then a statement on the 2nd of September, '95, to the investigators of the Prosecution; then a statement on the 26th of January, 1997; and then on the 26th of May this year, after the hearing of this case had already started. Only then, in this last statement, which you made seven years and six days after the killing of Samir Trako, you mentioned for the first time that Mario Cerkez was wearing a black uniform. How come you never said that before?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, maybe I wasn't asked that question before during the examination here, but I do know that evening there were three meetings, not just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Nobody asked you that. Mr. Kavazovic, let us go on to another topic now. You told us that by order of Miroslav Bralo, known as Cicko, you were taken to the health centre in Busovaca and then from there to the Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: From the first-aid or Emergency department in Busovaca, when they gave me medical treatment, infusion and some other shots, and then a nurse, I think she was called Marija --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Never mind. So from the first-aid station in Busovaca, you were taken to the former barracks called Draga?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, not Draga. No, the camp. Draga is behind Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The camp Seliste?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the warehouses of the Territorial Defence at Kaonik. I'm afraid I don't understand anything anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Allow me to ask you. Do you think that these localities that you have mentioned -- Draga, Seliste, and the Kaonik camp -- are one and the same place?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not one and the same place. Kaonik is where I was held in the camp; Seliste is where I was in the Bungalow; and Draga is quite a different barracks, behind Busovaca. I was never there. Now it is a barracks of the Federation army, or rather it was the HVO, now the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you are telling me, but 20 minutes ago, you said that from the Busovaca medical centre you were taken to the Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, Kaonik. Kaonik. I couldn't have been taken to the Draga barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Be that as it may, tell us, Mr. Kavazovic, the building that you were detained in in Kaonik, was it divided up into cells inside?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. There were rooms with two walls; there were nine or ten rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit Z1874.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, how long do you think you might be in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Another five minutes, on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This was an exhibit tendered today, if that can be of any assistance. Mr. Kavazovic, will you look at the second page of this exhibit. Tell us what it represents, this drawing of yours.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: This drawing represents the building in which I was detained at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. The numbers indicate the numbers of the cells, don't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you say, Mr. Kavasovic, that that building was in the middle of the circle that you drew on page 4 of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is in the middle, but I was in room number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavasovic, were you personally able to see the interior of the other buildings within the compound?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Except for this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any other building from the inside?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: From the inside, no, but I went out once to help to load sand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, you told us about that. Mr. Kavasovic, please don't misunderstand me, but I'm asking you this for procedural reasons. A moment ago you told us that after these events that you've testified to, that you were in hospital, that you had some psychiatric problems, and that you were there under examination. Will you tell us how you feel in that respect today? What is your condition today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: My condition, ever since I left the camp in 1993, I went for consultations with a neuropsychiatrist, but otherwise I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that. My last question,

utterances.speaker: MR. KAVASOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, who was the commander of the municipal HVO staff? Was that Marijan Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer? Could you be more specific regarding the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: June or July 1992.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Marijan Skopljak was linked to the police administration, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavasovic, may I just remind you, maybe you're confusing Pero and Marijan Skopljak. I'm asking you about Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kavasovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the International Tribunal to give evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will sit tomorrow at 10.15 and go on until 4.45.
